stem: The table most directly shows that between 1896 and 1900, Black voter registration in Louisiana

options.text: rose steadily as more Black men reached voting age
stayed roughly the same while white registration fell
collapsed, falling from over 130,000 to about 5,000
grew faster than white voter registration

rationales.A: The numbers fall every year; nothing rises.
rationales.B: Black registration falls far more steeply than white registration.
rationales.C: The Black column falls from 130,344 in 1896 to 12,902 in 1898 and 5,320 in 1900. That is a collapse of more than 95 percent in four years.
rationales.D: White registration ends at 125,437, far above the Black figure.
rationales.general:
1. Read the Black column. 130,344, then 12,902, then 5,320.
2. Read the direction. Down, steeply, at every step.
3. Compare with the white column. White registration dips and recovers; Black registration does not.
4. Match the change. A fall of more than 95 percent is a collapse, not a wobble.
Remember: a table’s story is in the direction and the size of the change.

stimulus.source_note: Louisiana voter registration, 1896–1900. Figures from the Historic New Orleans Collection (64 Parishes) and the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights briefing paper, Barriers to Voting in Louisiana (2018).
stimulus.text:
| Year | Black voters registered | White voters registered |
| 1896 | 130,344 | 164,088 |
| 1898 | 12,902 | 74,133 |
| 1900 | 5,320 | 125,437 |

Source: Louisiana voter registration figures, 1896–1900. Louisiana adopted a new constitution in 1898 with a poll tax, a literacy test, a property requirement, and a grandfather clause.
